rows.text: Installable user service, login startup and clean intentional shutdown.
rows.evidence: TICKED 2026-09-11 on a live run against the real account, recorded in docs/benchmarks/service-lifecycle-and-suspend.json with predictions registered beforehand. Clean stop: the unit logged its own unmount and exited in 38 ms, Result=success. Login startup: the user manager started it at 06:08:47.493, active 17.65 s after boot and ready and mounted 80 ms later, with Linger=no for this user, so no user manager and no default.target exist without a login -- the start is attributable to the [Install] section alone. Unchanged across the reboot: 184,052 indexed items, schema 7, 28 mount entries, both feeds reconnected, one FUSE mount owned by the new process, NRestarts=0. LIMIT: reads through the mount afterwards were served from the surviving on-disk cache, so they evidence the mount rather than the content path; the provider path is evidenced by Graph traffic, the reconnected feeds and a token refresh at 06:10:19.
rows.asserted_by: cirrove-service tests/packaging.rs holds the packaged unit to the wiring the live reboot depended on: enabling_the_unit_wires_it_into_the_login_session asserts [Install] WantedBy=default.target, which is the whole of the login-startup clause -- without it `systemctl --user enable` links nothing and the unit still reports as enabled. the_service_paths_are_user_relative_rather_than_one_developers_home asserts %h/%t specifiers and RuntimeDirectory 0700, so the evidence transfers past the one machine that produced it; an absolute /home path fails it. a_stop_leaves_time_to_unmount_before_it_is_killed asserts TimeoutStopSec is long enough to unmount before SIGKILL, and hardening_does_not_block_the_setuid_mount_helper asserts NoNewPrivileges is not set, which would stop fusermount3 at a user's next login and nowhere earlier. rows.text: Recovery after process failure, suspend/resume and loss of network access.
rows.evidence: Two of three clauses are test-covered; see asserted_by. CORRECTED 2026-09-10: this field previously named docs/benchmarks/namespace-memory-attribution.json, a heap-attribution artifact with no bearing on recovery -- a copy artifact from generating the ledger. CORRECTED AGAIN 2026-09-11: it then said the suspend/resume clause is unmeasured, which had stopped being true. It was measured (docs/benchmarks/service-lifecycle-and-suspend.json): the daemon came back from a suspend as the same process, same MainPID and ActiveEnterTimestamp, mount and index intact. That run's own verdict is why the row is still open, and it is a better reason than 'unmeasured': the cycle was two seconds of s2idle, too short to expire a token, tear down a network or lapse a subscription. A real access token lives about an hour and a measured subscription held 2,999,973 ms. So the shallow end of the clause holds and the end that matters is untested. Registered for the run that would close it: docs/benchmarks/deep-suspend-beyond-token-lifetime.json -- deep S3 rather than s2idle (this machine supports it; mem_sleep reads '[s2idle] deep', so the earlier run was shallow by setting and not by hardware, which that artifact had inferred wrongly), 90 minutes via rtcwake, and delivery of a change made after the wake. scripts/suspend-check.py captures the before state and compares it after, because a process on the machine being suspended cannot observe its own suspend. UPDATE 2026-09-13: process failure and network loss are now seen on a real desktop, not only in tests: an Ubuntu 24.04.4 VM with a signed-in OneDrive (docs/benchmarks/vm-recovery-and-real-desktop.json). SIGKILL of the daemon -> systemd restart, ready in 13s. The cable pulled for three minutes -> both feeds offline, the mount listing locally throughout, ready again 116s after the cable returned, the journal naming the stop and the return. A power cut (QMP quit) with a save one second old -> the journal opened and remounted ready in ~80s. One finding worth its own fix: the save caught in flight ended 'failed' (its payload not yet durable) and is not counted by stuck_changes, so it shows only in Recent activity, not in the attention count or tray -- P5 in that artifact. The suspend/resume clause is still the deep-suspend run below. TICKED 2026-09-14. The suspend clause is closed by a ninety-minute deep suspend on the Fedora VM -- registered 2026-09-11 and never run, because ninety minutes of the development machine is a morning, and a VM with a read-only account costs nobody anything. Deep confirmed by reading /sys/power/mem_sleep back, rtcwake scheduling the wake so the duration is a number, and CLOCK_BOOTTIME minus CLOCK_MONOTONIC moving 5400.1 s so the freeze was real. All five predictions hold: same MainPID, ActiveEnterTimestamp and boot id, so frozen rather than restarted; the mount intact and still serving 26 entries with a correct read through it; 'Microsoft authorization refreshed and saved' in the journal five seconds before the wake completed, with no prompt and the account never leaving ready; both subscriptions lapsed and renewed, after which a change made on another machine's mount of the same drive arrived in 6 s -- inside the thirty-second poll, so the subscription carried it and not the fallback; and indexed_items unchanged at 184053. See docs/benchmarks/deep-suspend-beyond-token-lifetime.json.
rows.asserted_by: Two of its three clauses. Process failure: tests/read_only.rs real_manager_recovers_disconnected_mount_after_process_death kills the mount process and asserts the manager reconnects, and real_manager_exits_with_client_handles_open covers the reverse. Loss of network access: the capacity fixtures' offline_remount phase remounts with the provider unreachable and asserts foreground_requests and content_reads both stay at zero, and tests/read_only.rs real_local_saves_remain_readable_during_upload_and_after_offline_restart covers the writable side. rows.text: Real token expiry/refresh and visible reauthentication when consent expires.
rows.evidence: Partial: the installed daemon refreshed its Microsoft grant hourly for 1.5 days without intervention (journal, 2026-09-07..09), which evidences real token refresh. The visible half is now covered end to end by tests rather than at its last hop only. CORRECTED 2026-09-11: this field said consent expiry 'cannot be scheduled'. Waiting for a grant to lapse on Microsoft's timetable cannot; REVOKING it can, and from the daemon's side that is the same event -- the token stops working and no refresh will fix it. Registered in docs/benchmarks/revoked-grant-and-reauthentication.json, with the clauses that matter beyond the state itself: that it is visible without reading a log, that the mount and the offline copies survive a credential problem, and that reauth restores the account without resetting the index or dropping pins. RUN 2026-09-13 (docs/benchmarks/revoked-grant-and-reauthentication.json), and the row is still not ticked. What was measured, against a real account: a refused grant is noticed without intervention and made visible without a log -- the tray reached NeedsAttention with the tooltip 'work-onedrive: sign-in required' -- and the mount, the cached listing and the pinned file all survived it, the pinned file reading in full to its checksum while access was refused. Recovery was automatic: re-enabling sign-in was enough, refresh succeeded at 09:29:39 and both feeds were ready by 09:30:40, with indexed_items, the pin and the cached listing unchanged against a reference taken before the withdrawal. WHY IT IS STILL OPEN: two things the run deliberately did not reach. The grant was WITHDRAWN by disabling the enterprise application's sign-in rather than by revoking consent, because the app has no verified publisher and re-consent could have needed an administrator; that tests the same daemon-side event and less of the consent cycle. And because recovery was automatic, `cirrove reauth` restoring an account was never exercised -- the better outcome for a user and the weaker one for this clause. A SEPARATE CONCERN FOUND BY THE RUN: the daemon wrote no journal entry at all when authorization was refused. The state reaches a user through the tray and `cirrove status`, which is what this row asks, but an operator reading the journal sees a healthy daemon and nothing says what the provider refused or why. CORRECTION 2026-09-14: the separate concern above -- that the daemon wrote no journal entry when authorization was refused -- does not hold as written. engine::feed_notice emits a warning on every transition into a state that is neither ready nor indexing, naming the collection, the state and the reason, and that includes sign_in_required. Observed on the Fedora VM the same morning: 'a collection stopped updating collection=... state=sign_in_required reason="sign-in required"'. An operator reading the journal does see it. What the 2026-09-13 run met was most likely a daemon that started already refused, so there was no transition to announce -- which is a narrower gap and a different one. WHAT KEEPS THIS ROW OPEN, unchanged: a withdrawal by revoking consent rather than disabling the application, and `cirrove reauth` actually restoring an account, which the last run never reached because recovery was automatic. Both need the account owner. CLOSED 2026-09-15. The two things that kept this row open were done, both by the account owner at the keyboard: the consent itself was revoked -- all six delegated permissions under the tenant's admin consent, not the application's sign-in toggle -- and `reauth` was actually exercised, from the window's own Sign in again button rather than the command line. The number the row never had: 66 minutes from the revocation to the daemon noticing, 68.5 from the issue of the token it held. That is one access-token lifetime and it is not ours to shorten; an access token is a signed assertion validated by expiry, not by asking whether consent still stands. Through that hour the daemon kept working correctly on data it was still entitled to, both feeds succeeding every few seconds. Then both moved to sign_in_required with a journal warning each -- which also closes what the 2026-09-11 run found and could not fix at the time, that the daemon changed state and wrote nothing. The window showed 'Erneut anmelden'; the sign-in re-consented; the mount came down at 21:20:01 and back at 21:20:56, deliberately, because reauthentication disables the account so its workers release the old credential; ready at 21:21:22 with 184,080 items, the same number as before, no reindex. The pin half was not retested here -- this account held none at the time -- and is covered by the first run.
rows.asserted_by: The refresh half: cirrove-auth tests simultaneous_expiry_rotates_once_and_stale_401_cannot_expire_new_token, credentials_are_not_used_when_rotation_cannot_be_persisted, and explicitly_granted_write_scope_survives_refresh_and_keyring_roundtrip. The visible half is now whole: read_only::an_expired_grant_is_shown_as_needing_sign_in_and_not_as_being_offline drives a provider that refuses the grant and asserts the feed reaches sign_in_required -- with an unreachable provider first as the control, so a daemon that called everything sign_in_required would fail it; manager::tests::a_feed_needing_sign_in_is_not_hidden_by_one_that_is_merely_offline holds the ordering into the account state a caller reads, and fails if a noisier feed is allowed to win; and cirrove-desktop/tests/accounts.rs renders that state. Each was shown to fail without its subject. NOT ASSERTED: the revocation itself, which needs a person and is registered rather than claimed. The event itself is not assertable by a test and never will be: it needs a person to revoke a consent in a tenant. docs/benchmarks/revoked-grant-and-reauthentication.json carries both runs, what each withdrew and what each could not reach.

rows.text: Responsive navigation during initial indexing and competing downloads.
rows.evidence: docs/benchmarks/navigation-stall-cause.json Live 2026-09-09 on a real 184,000-item linked collection, cold-indexed (docs/validation.md#navigating-a-real-collection-while-it-is-being-indexed, benchmarks/live-navigation-during-indexing.json): first visits to directories not seen before measure p50 192.1 ms and p95 317.0 ms while indexing, and p50 210.5 ms with p95 435.3 ms under a competing download, across 375 directories with no failed listing. The 500 ms threshold the fixture asserts against is exceeded once in 132 samples without a download and six times in 243 with one. STILL OPEN: the tail, not the median. A companion run that re-listed one directory reported p50 1.3 ms and is not evidence for this box, because a directory listed every 250 ms stays active and is refreshed in the background. REPLICATED 2026-09-10 on a separate validation connection, a different day and a different build: p50 177.8-193.7 ms against 192.1-210.5, and the competing download raises p95 by a factor of 1.36 against 1.37. The median reproduces closely. The tail is worse, not better -- maximum 1184.9 ms against 834.5, and 8 to 12 samples over 500 ms rather than 6. See docs/benchmarks/live-navigation-during-indexing.json. WHY IT IS STILL OPEN, stated properly 2026-09-11: not for want of measurement. The row says 'responsive' and names no number, and the only bound in the code is a sixty-second give-up deadline, so the clause cannot be failed -- which live-navigation-during-indexing.json said itself in its decision rule before it ran. The 500 ms the fixture asserts is for CACHED navigation; a first visit necessarily costs a provider round trip that cached navigation does not, and no threshold was ever declared for it. Reframed and registered in docs/benchmarks/navigation-interference.json: the clause is 'during initial indexing and competing downloads', so the question is interference, not speed -- p95 of a first visit in each arm against an IDLE, fully indexed control on the same machine and network, which has never been run. A ratio removes the provider and the network, which this project does not control. Bounded at twice the idle arm, plus a hard five-second ceiling on any single listing, because the tail is what a person calls a freeze and a percentile cannot see it. The registration records that one arm's answer is already known (the download factor, 1.37 replicated at 1.36) and carries it as a check that the method reproduces; the indexing factor is the unknown the bound was set for. UPDATE 2026-09-15: the registered navigation-interference run was made, three times, on the Fedora VM against the owner's real 184,076-item drive, and it found two defects in its own fixture before it found anything about the daemon. The three arms shared one directory tree and the first two ate it -- the collection has 1,548 directories and the busy arms visited all of them, leaving the control arm two samples -- so each arm now takes a budget of samples rather than a slice of time. And the arm labelled 'with a competing download' had no evidence that anything was competing: at one stream it moved 1.75 MiB/s and its p95 came out BELOW the arm without it (0.84 where two host runs had measured 1.36 and 1.37). The validator now counts the bytes the transfer moves. At six streams, 220 MB at 7.79 MiB/s, the interference reappears: p95 274 ms alone against 336 ms competing, a factor of 1.23. THE CONTROL ARM EXISTS AT LAST: a settled, fully indexed daemon answers a first visit in 5.4 ms at the median and 8.4 ms at p95, against 179 ms and 274 ms while the index is being built -- which says the difference is where the answer comes from, not contention, and that the registered P2 (indexing under twice idle) was asking the wrong question. Slowest listing in any arm: 486 ms, against the registered five-second ceiling, with no failed listing anywhere. STILL OPEN, by the artifact's own decision rule: P3 did not reproduce, so the run is repeated rather than interpreted. What closes this row is named in the artifact -- an absolute ceiling on a first visit during the index build and an interference factor against a transfer whose rate is declared in advance -- and both are met by these numbers, which is exactly why they must be registered before the run rather than after. docs/benchmarks/navigation-interference.json. CLOSED 2026-09-16 on a registration written the same morning, before the runs, with bounds that could fail for the right reason -- docs/benchmarks/navigation-during-the-first-index.json, which supersedes navigation-interference.json and says why: that one asked the indexing arm's p95 to be under twice the IDLE arm's, and those are not two measurements of one thing. Three runs of the same method on the Fedora VM against the owner's real 184,000-item drive, each a cold engine indexing from nothing. A first visit during the first index: p95 291, 238 and 283 ms against a bound of 500; worst single listing 712 ms against a ceiling of five seconds; not one failure in 360 samples. Once the index is built the same walk costs 5 to 6 ms at the median. A competing transfer of 8.3 to 9.3 MiB/s never pushed the p95 past a doubling. THE SPREAD IS PART OF THE RESULT and is recorded rather than averaged away: the interference factor came out 2.00, 1.15 and 0.78 at nearly constant load, and in the third run the arm with the transfer was faster than the arm without. So the clause is met, and no single interference factor may be quoted from this -- the effect is inside the method's noise. The first run alone read 1.9955 against a bound of 2, a margin of 0.45 percent against a method that varies by fifteen; the two repeats are what turned that coin flip into a bound three runs agree on.
rows.asserted_by: filesystem::capacity::real_combined_namespace_churn, churn.rs:403 -- read: asserts cached navigation stays under 500 ms while committed changes are being applied, on every round. Supported by content::windows::tests::graph::kernel fixtures covering navigation during a stalled transfer. The measurement is a fixture rather than a test and cannot run in CI: it needs a live account and twelve minutes of indexing. `cirrove validate-onedrive-navigation --per-arm 60 --streams 6 --idle-seconds 60` reproduces it on any machine with an account, and refuses its own second arm if the competing transfer moved too little to count.

All four clauses are now evidenced on a live mount. Per-cache-block metadata checks: conservative Graph metadata GETs track content GETs at about two per block (22 against 10, and 7 against 3 at a four-fold smaller size) while the optimized path does not (4 against 4, 3 against 2), each arm on its own cold engine directory with counters sampled around the read alone. Bytes are SHA-256 identical through the kernel mount at both sizes, with the optimized arm asserted to have bound a session and the conservative arm asserted not to. Shared setup and bounded windows: setups 1 and conditional_windows 3 on a live mount. Safe renewal: renewals 1 under continuous reading across the 60 s lease; an idle pause does not reach it because the read after it is served outside the session. NOT TICKED, and not for want of evidence: conditional_reads is false by default, so a shipped daemon still performs the per-block checks measured absent here. Enabling it is a product decision. rows.text: Push-triggered metadata updates, reconnection/catch-up and periodic recovery checks, with provider delivery and local reaction latency measured separately.
rows.evidence: docs/validation.md#push-notifications and #subscription-renewal-at-the-real-boundary -- live 2026-09-09: delivery 30.0-32.7 s across eleven samples, local reaction 169-287 ms, measured separately as the box requires. One subscription held 2,999,973 ms, renewed, reconnected, and delivered a fresh change 30,441 ms later. One notification in eleven was never delivered (90 s deadline); the pre-registered interference hypothesis was refuted by an immediately passing retry and the miss stands unexplained; the shipped 30 s poll bounds the impact. Catch-up and periodic recovery are now covered live too (docs/validation.md#catch-up-after-a-reconnection-and-the-periodic-recovery-refresh, benchmarks/live-catchup-and-recovery.json, 2026-09-09): a change made with nothing connected and the poll an hour away was fetched 408 ms after the subscription connected and listed 206 ms later; with no subscription at all the 30 s poll found one in 29,421 ms. Each phase disabled the other and counted zero directory listings before its delta, so neither is explained by activity revalidation. RENEWAL OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-11: the validator held a real Socket.IO subscription for its full lifetime, Microsoft renewed it, and a change made afterwards was delivered through the renewed connection -- 'Renewed subscription connected; checking a new change through it' followed by a passing delivery. That is a renewal the provider performed rather than one a fixture simulated. STILL OPEN: the one notification in eleven that was never delivered remains unexplained; the periodic figure bounds its impact rather than accounting for it. REPLICATED 2026-09-10 on a separate write-grant validation connection, a different day and build. Catch-up: delta 1536 ms after the subscription connected against 408 ms first time, entry listed 206 ms later -- the same figure to the millisecond. Periodic recovery: delta 29,454 ms against 29,421, a difference of 33 ms across two independent runs. Directory freshness through a real mount: three rounds at 5,147 / 5,297 / 5,103 ms total from change to visible, which is the five-second activity revalidation interval and not push. A mounted view following remote changes: create visible in 2 ms, move in 4,650 ms, delete in 4,450 ms.
rows.asserted_by: tests/read_only.rs::push_refreshes_immediately_and_retains_bursts_during_an_active_delta covers push-triggered refresh and burst coalescing during an active delta; push_preserves_retry_after_and_reconnect_catches_unreported_changes covers the reconnection/catch-up clause and the provider's retry-after; real_push_updates_the_mounted_namespace_without_waiting_for_polling covers the same through a kernel mount with polling out of the way. NOT ASSERTED BY ANY TEST: the clause 'provider delivery and local reaction latency measured separately'. No unit test can measure a real provider's delivery latency; that clause rests on the live runs recorded in docs/validation.md, and one notification in eleven was never delivered and is still unexplained.

rows.text: Bounded memory and background work with large libraries and long sessions.
rows.evidence: docs/benchmarks/namespace-trim-closes-g3.json 2026-09-10: this box cannot be answered without naming the allocator. docs/benchmarks/daemon-allocator-arenas.json measured the live daemon reading 475 MB from cache: with default glibc arenas it rests at 211.3 MiB after two passes and returns essentially none of what each pass takes; capped at one arena, 107.9 MiB. The user's long-running daemon was at 338.4 MiB. Any bound stated without fixing that setting is a bound on a coin flip. WHAT IS ACTUALLY IN THE WAY, 2026-09-11: a product decision nobody has made, and it was deferred for a good reason -- daemon-allocator-arenas.json measured the memory half and said so: 'it trades resident memory against allocator concurrency, and the second half has not been measured at all'. That second half is now registered (docs/benchmarks/allocator-arena-cost.json): what capping costs in wall-clock completion and in p95 of a single read, as a ratio, with bounds set before the run. Also names an inconsistency that should not survive the decision either way: CI already pins MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1 for the mounted read workloads -- 'without the cap the RSS assertion measures glibc arena retention' -- while the shipped systemd unit sets no allocator environment at all. So a memory assertion passes in CI under conditions the product does not reproduce. UPDATE 2026-09-14: the product decision this row was waiting on is made, and made on both halves of the trade rather than on one. docs/benchmarks/allocator-arena-cost.json ran the registered arms: six workload and latency combinations per arm, identical bytes and identical provider requests in every pair, so the comparison is about the allocator. Capping costs at worst 2.1% of wall-clock and 3.2% of a single read's p95 -- and three of six combinations were faster capped. Growth is 43.9 to 44.6 MiB capped against 103.0 to 158.1 default, with the spread falling from 55.1 MiB to 0.7. The shipped unit now sets Environment=MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1 and a test holds it there, which also closes the inconsistency named here: CI pinned the setting while the product did not, so a memory measurement was passing under conditions the shipped daemon never reproduced. The default arm could not even be run before this: the fixture refused to start without the cap, so the trade could not be measured with the workload it is a trade about. STILL NOT DONE: the bound itself, stated against the capped allocator, over a long session with a large library -- which is now a measurement with no decision in front of it.

rows.text: Reclaim inactive namespace views with correct FUSE lifetimes; pass the 500,000-file traversal, invalidation and 24-hour churn memory gates in [namespace memory](adr/0005-namespace-memory.md). Content-cache limits do not satisfy this requirement.
rows.evidence: CORRECTED 2026-09-11: this field named only docs/benchmarks/namespace-memory-attribution.json, the 2026-09-08 attribution run, and so still described a gate that has since closed. G3 -- released PSS minus indexed baseline, at most 256 MiB -- failed at 476.4 / 514.8 / 546.7 MiB and now reads 13.3 / 16.1 / 16.3 (docs/benchmarks/namespace-trim-closes-g3.json, 2026-09-10). The reclamation tick returns the pages once a mount has shed its views and gone quiet, which was the plausible outcome all along: 96.4-96.8 percent of the retained RSS was allocator-held free arena and not live data. It is a hard assertion in the fixture now, not a reported number. WHAT REMAINS, and it is not addressed by trimming at all: the traversal PEAK. traversed_with_old_files holds 492.8 / 490.7 / 504.1 MiB at 750,438 live views, and returning pages afterwards cannot lower a high-water mark reached while the views were held. Only shedding does. The number that work turns on is 637-657 bytes per live view, which reproduces to within 0.2 percent while retained RSS varies by 6 percent -- so a peak budget is a budget on concurrent live views, and at 650 bytes each a 256 MiB peak buys about 413,000 against the 750,438 held here. Two further gates in ADR 0005 are also unmet and neither is a measurement: G2 needs an evictable-bytes counter that does not exist, and G7's plateau tolerance must be fixed from a two-hour pilot before its twenty-four-hour run. THE PEAK HAS NO LIVE DESIGN, and that is the honest state rather than a gap in effort: two have been written and both were killed by their own gating measurement. Shedding -- emit notify_inval_entry above a ceiling -- needed about 1,400 per second to bind during a traversal and sustains about 107 under concurrent lookups (inval-entry-rate.json, 2026-09-08). Its successor ADR 0006, shortening the entry TTL above a ceiling so the kernel's own dentry reclamation does the work, is marked 'rejected by its own measurement' (2026-09-09): the peak does not move. ADR 0005 carried both the retirement and, in a later paragraph, the claim that the measurement had never been taken; corrected 2026-09-12. What is left is named there and neither half is small: reduce bytes per view, which three passes have moved 15-20 percent each and which will not reach a factor of two alone, or decline to resolve views beyond a ceiling at all -- a change to the lookup contract rather than to reclamation, which needs its own ADR and does not have one.

rows.text: Real restart/outage checks and at least 24 hours of sustained operation.
rows.evidence: TICKED 2026-09-14. Attempt 2 ran the full 24.0 hours in the Ubuntu VM -- 1440 samples, no void or probe-lost marker -- and all five registered predictions hold. The mount was present in every one of the 1440 samples. Memory stayed flat, 42 to 43 MiB on the first run and 40 to 42 on the second, peak 43 MiB, segmented by pid because comparing across a restart reports the restart as growth. The index held between 184,053 and 184,054, the extra one being the file written after the outage. The slowest root listing of the entire day was 7 ms against a ceiling of 1000 and the mean was 1.0 ms -- including all twenty-five samples where the account read updating_or_offline, where the mount was present every time and the slowest listing was 1 ms, which is the clause's whole point: a listing served from the local namespace does not wait on the provider. Both injections recovered unattended: the restart at four hours in 10 s, and a five-minute link outage with both feeds back to ready 95 s after the cable returned, a file written afterwards uploaded in 10 s and confirmed in the cloud through Graph. Attempt 1 on the owner's machine was void when removing the packages took /usr/bin/cirrove with it; that is why the sampler now refuses to start blind. See docs/benchmarks/sustained-operation.json and the samples beside it.
rows.asserted_by: scripts/sustained-operation-report.py answers each of the five registered predictions from the sample file and refuses a file carrying a void or probe-lost marker, so the artifact cannot be read as a result if the window was compromised. rows.text: Crash/fault tests at every durable transition and concurrent remote edits.
rows.evidence: docs/benchmarks/durable-transition-crash-coverage.json and durable-transition-sites.json for process death: all 31 runtime durable transitions are crossed by a process that then dies, measured rather than read. 2026-09-11, faults below the process: docs/benchmarks/journal-under-io-faults.json. A dm-flakey device switched to error_writes at runtime and back. What was durable before the fault survives it and reads back byte for byte afterwards; new work is refused as JournalError::Storage rather than as corruption -- reporting a refusing device as a corrupt journal would send a user to recovery steps that destroy work the device still holds. A prediction failed usefully: the journal cannot be OPENED on a failing device, because opening opens SQLite and SQLite writes. So its contents are inaccessible during a fault, which is not the same as lost, and the run makes only the second claim. A LYING FSYNC ran the same day: dm-flakey drop_writes acknowledges the write and discards it, and the journal detected it -- sealing was refused as JournalError::Stale, because the journal reads back what it wrote and finds the generation unchanged. Work durable before the lie reads back byte for byte afterwards. The claim is that this injection did not produce wrong-and-confident data, not that no discard can. TORN WRITES were attempted and are inconclusive: corrupt_bio_byte flips a byte in EVERY write bio, so it corrupts ext4's metadata as readily as the journal's data, and the phase hung. A hang in that state is a statement about ext4 meeting corrupted metadata, not about the journal. The targeted version of the same question is already answered -- overwriting a sealed payload makes recovery fail. THE POWER CUT WAS RUN on 2026-09-13 and holds (docs/benchmarks/journal-under-power-cut.json): 585 generations acknowledged durable, the machine's power removed mid-write, and afterwards the journal opened, produced generation 585 byte for byte, and sealed new work again. Verified as a real power loss rather than a reboot: the previous boot's journal ends mid-kernel-message with no shutdown sequence. PREVIOUSLY RECORDED AS STILL OPEN: The fixture for it now exists and is registered in docs/benchmarks/journal-under-power-cut.json -- seed writes ~68 acknowledged generations a second and never stops, so a cut cannot land on an idle journal, and recover asserts that everything acknowledged before the cut reads back byte for byte and that the journal takes new work again. It was exercised against process death first, which proves the mechanics and nothing about durability, and it was shown to FAIL when the acknowledged payload is altered or removed. What is left is a person and a power cut; that is the whole of what this box still needs, and it is why it is not ticked.

rows.evidence:
TICKED 2026-09-11. Scope expanded by the user on 2026-09-09. COVERED end to end. Preservation: a refused save leaves the sealed payload and the dirty working copy intact. rows.text: Defined filename, package/notebook and unsupported-operation behavior.
rows.evidence: PARTIAL 2026-09-13. Filename behaviour is defined and enforced at the mount: the provider states its rules (ReadProvider::name_problem; OneDrive's in cirrove_onedrive::naming -- the forbidden characters, leading/trailing spaces, a trailing period, device names with or without extension, ~$, _vti_, .lock, desktop.ini, 255 characters) and mkdir, create and rename answer EINVAL or ENAMETOOLONG before anything is journalled, where before such a name was accepted, uploaded, refused by Graph and left as a stuck change. Documented for users in docs/user-guide.md. The unsupported operations and their errnos are stated in docs/compatibility.md (links and special files ENOSYS, xattr reads ENODATA and an empty list, xattr writes ENOSYS, mode/owner changes EOPNOTSUPP, non-regular creates EOPNOTSUPP, .Trash EOPNOTSUPP, rename flags EOPNOTSUPP). NOT DONE: package/notebook behaviour -- OneNote sections and .one packages are folders to Graph and files to a person, and nothing yet decides what the mount shows. TICKED 2026-09-14. The package clause is decided and enforced rather than left open. A OneNote notebook is a folder to Graph and one thing to a person, and what is under it are section files only OneNote can write. The mount shows the contents -- a person can list, read and copy them -- and refuses every change inside, at any depth, with EOPNOTSUPP. Refused before anything is journalled, because the provider would refuse it anyway and a change that gets that far becomes a stuck change while the mount already shows it as done, which is the failure this project met once with fourteen folder removals. The fact is carried on the node rather than as a fourth NodeKind, so every match on kind is not made to answer a question it does not care about, and it is skipped when serializing so the stored form of an ordinary node is byte-for-byte unchanged -- an index of 184,000 nodes is not rewritten to record that almost none of them are notebooks. Documented in compatibility.md and the user guide.

rows.text: Deletion defined end to end: the provider's recycle bin as the default for every file manager without an extension, no local wastebasket created inside the user's drive, permanent deletion reachable only as an explicit second gesture that the window offers too, and both gated on a per-provider capability so a provider without a recycle bin is never presented as recoverable. One clause of five is closed: the mount root refuses to hold a local wastebasket, in both ways one can appear -- mkdir refuses to create it, rename refuses to fill an existing one. Found as a real directory -- .Trash-1000/ with files/ and info/, created by GNOME Files at 17:57 in a live OneDrive on a writable mount -- not from reading the specification, and confirmed as a remote create in the mutation journal rather than a local shadow. Verified on the live mount after installing the guard: both names refused with EOPNOTSUPP, an ordinary folder still creatable. rows.release_note: The tray is an optional surface by the project's own rule: no control or state may be reachable only through it, and everything it offers is in the window. What is left is recent activity in the tray menu, which is its own row.
rows.evidence: PARTIAL 2026-09-11. The tray's icon, tooltip and SNI Status are the daemon's answer over the subscribe stream and nothing inferred from it; losing the service is rendered rather than hidden, because a tray keeping its last icon after the daemon is gone reports something it does not know. Seen working on the user's own panel. The menu gives each account a submenu with Open folder and Mount/Unmount, and the toggle is decided from current state at click time rather than from what was drawn. Mounting goes through accounts::set_enabled_by_id, the same locked call the window and CLI make; it was held back for a while on a claim that a second writer would race the window over the settings file, which was wrong -- the configuration and per-account operation locks were already there. NOT DONE: recent activity is its own box (line 281), and the failure notice is a tooltip rather than anything a user is shown without hovering. TWO THINGS A REAL LOGIN FOUND, 2026-09-13. First: the tray did not start at login and the autostart entry was installed correctly. systemd-xdg-autostart-generator resolves Exec= against its own PATH, which at session start does not include ~/.local/bin, so it logged 'executable specified in Exec= does not exist' and wrote no unit -- silently, with nothing reaching the user. The shipped bare Exec= is right for a package in /usr/bin (limine-restore-notify sits beside it with a bare Exec and generates fine) and wrong for a user-local install, which must rewrite it to an absolute path. Verified by running the generator by hand before and after: no unit, then app-io.github.Dandiccf.Cirrove.Tray@autostart.service. This is why the login-start clause existed and it failed on its first real test. Second: a user cannot eject the mount from a file manager at all -- fusermount3 -u and gio mount -u both refuse with 'target is busy' while nothing user-visible holds it. The supported path works and unmounts in about two seconds, but 'target is busy' names nothing a person can act on, and the first person to try it concluded the drive remounts itself. See docs/desktop.md. FIXED 2026-09-13: scripts/install-tray-autostart.py resolves the binary against the generator's own PATH rather than the shell's, writes a bare Exec= when that resolves and an absolute one when it does not, and then runs the generator to confirm a unit comes out. Four tests hold the rule and three of them fail if it always writes the bare name, which is the shape of the original bug; wired into CI beside the other script tests.

rows.text: Nautilus badges, pin/unpin actions and consistent status refresh.
rows.evidence: PARTIAL 2026-09-13. The daemon answers a new `paths` verb -- up to 200 mount-relative paths per request, each with kind, pin cover (direct / inherited from a recursive folder pin / none) and bytes on disk -- so a file manager asks once per listing. packaging/nautilus/cirrove.py (nautilus-python) draws a badge on pinned items (check when the content is on disk, synchronising while fetching, none on the on-demand majority), adds a Cirrove column with the words, and offers Keep offline / Stop keeping offline on selections and folder backgrounds, recursive for folders; after an action it invalidates the item so Files asks again. Every call is off the UI thread with a 3 s timeout; no daemon or an older one draws nothing. Seen in a real Files window on this machine against the live daemon (Nautilus 50, nautilus-python 4.1): a check on a recursively pinned folder in both grid and list view, none on its on-demand neighbours, the pinned file at the mount root likewise; Files asks one entry at a time and the answers arrive within the same second for a seven-entry folder. Two wrong turns on the way, both recorded in docs/desktop.md#files: Python threads stand still inside Files, and the completion must name the provider Files passed in. NOT DONE: a refresh when a pin changes behind Files (the extension re-asks when Files re-lists or after its own actions, not on a daemon event), and the menu action exercised by hand. UPDATE 2026-09-13: the extension also implements Nautilus.PropertiesModelProvider, so Alt+Enter on a file shows a Cirrove section -- availability, bytes on this computer, whether a pin keeps it, cloud location, provider item id. The standard properties (size, MIME type, modified time, permissions) were verified correct on the live mount. UPDATE 2026-09-13 (badges): the badges are Cirrove's own icons rather than the desktop's generic ones -- a blue cloud with a check for kept and present, a cloud with a down arrow while content arrives (down because that is the direction; the tray's up arrow means a save on its way out), both with a white rim because Files draws them over a thumbnail of any colour. On this machine the generic emblem-ok-symbolic and emblem-synchronizing-symbolic resolved to a thin grey tick and circular arrow that said nothing about a cloud and did not match the tray. The generic names are still used where the branded icons are not installed, because Files draws nothing at all for a name no theme provides -- a missing badge, not a plain one. Checked against the live account: the extension resolves the branded names, a pinned file carries the kept badge and an on-demand neighbour none. UPDATE 2026-09-15 (the refresh clause): closed. Files asks about a path when it lists a directory and then keeps the answer, so a pin made in the window left an open Files window showing the opposite of the truth for as long as it was left open -- not a delay, a wrong badge with no expiry. The account event now carries `kept_generation`, a number that moves when what an account keeps offline changes: a pin made or released, or one of its files arriving. A number and not a path, because the channel carries none and a tray reads it too. The extension subscribes over GLib's asynchronous I/O -- the same reason everything else in it does, a Python thread inside Files runs only while the main thread is in a callback -- keeps a bounded registry of what it has badged, and invalidates that account's entries when the number moves. Priming is not a change, and a lagged stream treats everything as stale once. Seen on the owner's machine on 2026-09-15 with an open Files window on the drive: `cirrove pin` from a terminal, and the window logged `what is kept changed, refreshing 3 entries`, asked the daemon again about all three, and control.bin went from `On demand` to `Kept offline` with its badge, with nothing done in Files; unpinning took it back the same way. This also repairs what the job change would otherwise have broken here: keeping something offline now answers before the content arrives, so without a push the badge would have stayed on `not downloaded` forever. STILL NOT DONE: the menu action exercised by hand. Seen again on 2026-09-15 on a second machine and from a packaged install rather than a developer one: the Fedora VM upgraded from the r418 packages to r447, the account back at 184,076 items after the restart, Files open on the drive, and `cirrove pin` in a terminal moved control.bin from `On demand` to `Kept offline` with its badge inside ten seconds -- the journal shows the extension asking the daemon again without Files re-listing. First, the extension translated nothing: twenty-one hardcoded English strings in a German file manager, of which the German catalogue already knew one. The owner right-clicked three times looking for "Offline behalten", read past "Keep offline" each time, and reported that nothing was there -- three separate reports of a missing feature that was present. gettext is bound now and twenty translations are in po/de.po. Second, and found only because the label changed, `_item` decided keep-versus-un-keep with `text.startswith("Stop")`; the first translation would have turned every un-keep into a keep, silently. menu_label returns label and intent separately and a test asserts the intent against the state. Then, with German in place: right-click -> "Offline behalten" on a 139,703-byte PDF, badge appeared, the menu switched to "Nicht mehr offline behalten", and the daemon agreed -- one pin, 139,735 bytes reserved, kept_generation 2. `cirrove pins` then named it 01YQR2QYPXJNXJZ7LXENA2KXH77S2VBEFB, because relative_path stopped only at the account's own root and this account subscribes to two drives; every item in the other one had no path anywhere it was shown. Fixed with four tests, two of which fail without it. The file now reads "Unternehmen/Umlaufbeschlüsse/20220408 Umlaufbeschluss goodguys.pdf".

rows.text: Actionable errors, progress, cancellation and conflict resolution.
rows.evidence: PARTIAL 2026-09-11. Conflict resolution has its first real piece, and it was built because the daemon could strand a change in silence: fourteen folder removals ended in Conflict on a live drive, hiding the directories in the mount while leaving them in the account, with no status field saying so and no way to clear them -- request_mutation_retry refuses Conflict by design and nothing else touched one. AccountStatus.stuck_changes now reports them and `cirrove discard-stuck` abandons them. Measured end to end on that drive: 14 abandoned, 14 back in view, 10 deleted cleanly on the second attempt, 4 conflicted again on stale ETags and cleared after the delta feed caught up. Final state: no leftovers, nothing stuck. NOT DONE: removals only -- a stuck creation or move leaves the local tree depending on it and is refused rather than half-handled; discard only, never retry; no per-item view, so a user sees a count and not which paths; neither the window nor the tray shows it; and progress and cancellation are untouched. FIXED 2026-09-13: the count is no longer a number nobody reads. It travels on the event channel (Event::Account gained stuck_changes, serde(default) so an older daemon reads back as zero and an older client ignores the field), and the tray raises the icon to NeedsAttention, names it in the tooltip -- 'ready, 3 changes not applied', the healthy state beside it because that is what makes it surprising -- and offers 'Discard N changes the cloud refused' in the menu, shown only when there is something to discard. The menu entry calls discard-stuck over the control socket, which is allowed because it is a shortcut to a CLI command and not the only way there; leaving a user informed and helpless was the worse failure. NOT DONE still: no per-item view, so a user sees a count and not which paths, and the window shows nothing. UPDATE 2026-09-13: the count of refused changes and the Discard action are in the window as well as the tray: a 'Changes the cloud refused' row with the count, shown only while there is something to discard, and a Discard button that asks the daemon and reports what it could unwind. Progress and cancellation of transfers remain NOT DONE. UPDATE 2026-09-15 (progress and cancellation): both clauses are closed, and closing them turned up a defect rather than a gap. Keeping something offline ran the whole fetch inside the control request, and the client half of every verb gives up after three seconds -- so `cirrove pin --recursive` on a real folder reported `Cirrove pin timed out` while the daemon went on keeping every file. Measured on the owner's drive: 3.00 s to that message, and the daemon then kept all 69 files, 399 MB across 152 blocks. The person was told their request failed about work that had succeeded, and the window's Keep offline button used the same call, holding its one operation slot for the duration behind a spinner with no way to stop. Long work is now a job (docs/adr/0011-long-work-is-a-job.md): the request resolves, walks and reserves -- all local, all instant -- and answers with a job id; the fetch runs on the account's task tracker under a token that is a child of the account's. Progress rides in `status` beside the pins, read at answer time rather than from the five-second status loop, because a bar that moved five seconds ago is a spinner with extra steps. Measured after the change on the same account: 0.01 s to the reply on a fetch that then ran 9.66 s, with fifteen samples of `cirrove jobs` rising from 3 of 25 files and 713 KB to 24 of 25 and 42 MB of 51 MB. Stopping is the `stop-job` verb and a Stop button on the row: stopped 2.51 s into a 40-file folder, the command returned 0.01 s later naming how far it got, and the pin and its reservation were released -- someone who stopped a fetch did not ask to keep part of a folder. A fetch that fails instead protects what it kept and its row stays, carrying how far it got and why, until dismissed. Uploads report their progress too, from `transferred_bytes`, which the journal has always recorded and nothing ever showed. docs/benchmarks/keeping-a-folder-offline-as-a-job.json. STILL NOT DONE: conflict resolution, the row's fourth word -- refused changes can be discarded and never retried. Cancelling an upload is deliberately not offered: the bytes are already on the person's disk, so the only thing a cancel could mean is throwing their save away, which `discard-stuck` already does behind a confirmation that names the count. UPDATE 2026-09-15 (retry): 'discard only, never retry' is answered, and the answer is that there were always two kinds of refusal behind one number. A change that FAILED -- a quota, a permission, a connection that went away -- is one the cloud never decided about, and trying it again is ordinary. A change in CONFLICT is one the cloud did decide about: the remote moved, and re-sending would act on whatever is there now, which is how a rename nobody made or a deletion of a version nobody saw happens. `request_mutation_retry` has refused Conflict since it was written and nothing outside the journal had ever called it, so the distinction existed in the code and nowhere a person could reach. Now: `retry-stuck` over the control socket, `cirrove retry-stuck`, and a Try again button beside Discard in the window -- insensitive when every refusal is a conflict, rather than lying about what pressing it would do. The row's sentence changed with it: it used to read 'they will not be retried' about all of them, and now says how many are worth another try and why the rest are not. STILL NOT DONE: conflict resolution beyond this. A conflict can be tried again only by discarding it and making the change afresh; there is no keep-both, no side-by-side copy, and no way to see what the remote did instead. CLOSED 2026-09-16. The row's last sentence was "conflict resolution beyond this: a conflict can be tried again only by discarding it and making the change afresh; there is no keep-both, no side-by-side copy, and no way to see what the remote did instead". All three now exist. Keeping both puts the person's bytes beside the cloud's version under a new name -- Report (conflicted copy 2026-09-16).docx -- because a refused save keeps its payload in the journal, sealed and checked against its digest; the original becomes UploadState::Resolved, which is the first ending a conflicted save has ever had (nothing removed one before, so the owner had a power-cut test still counted days later). Reached by `cirrove keep-both`, the control socket, and a Keep both copies button on the window's unsent-saves row, which had no button at all because the only one that fitted would have been Discard. And what the remote did instead is shown: the size and date of the version the cloud has now, in the CLI listing and in the window row, because choosing between your version and theirs while being told nothing about theirs is a guess rather than a choice. Two earlier gaps in the same row closed the same day: failed saves are named rather than counted, and Try again reaches them. The copy's name is deliberately not translated -- it is a file name that travels to the cloud and back to every other machine -- and carries the date so a second conflict on one file cannot overwrite the first rescue.

With the window open on Arch/Hyprland, the compositor reports the window's app id as io.github.Dandiccf.Cirrove -- byte for byte the desktop entry's own name -- and reports it as a native Wayland client rather than one going through Xwayland. rows.text: Show recent activity -- remote changes from the delta feed and local saves from the upload journal, with each entry's state -- in the window, and a short form of it in the tray menu. "Recent" means changes to content, not files the user merely opened: a mount stages cache on every read, so a touched-files list would be noise. This is a log and not a level, so it does not ride the coalescing event channel, which by design hands a lagging client current state instead of the entries it missed; it needs its own query. File names appear in the menu and in the window, never in the tray tooltip, which is shown on hover without intent and is visible to anyone looking at the screen or a shared one; the tooltip carries a count. rows.evidence: PARTIAL 2026-09-13. The daemon records what the delta feed delivers from the second delta on -- the first lists the whole drive and a re-baseline does the same, and neither is activity -- in a bounded in-memory ring per account, with names (a deletion's name read from the index before the page publishes), and answers `recent` with those and the journal's latest saves, states included, item ids resolved to names through the index. The window shows a Recent activity group when there is anything, cloud changes first, the refused saves marked; the tray shows five lines under each account's entry, fetched after each account event; `cirrove recent` prints both. Seen live: a fresh daemon lists its journal's recent uploads. NOT DONE: the ring forgets on restart (by design, but the window then shows only the journal side until the feed moves); no times shown for local saves (the journal has none); nothing distinguishes added from changed, because the feed does not. UPDATE 2026-09-14: the times clause is closed. The upload journal had no timestamp at all, so the window could list what a person saved but never when -- and after a restart, with the remote ring empty by design, that left a column of saves against nothing and no way to tell this morning's from last week's. UploadRecord now carries saved_at, LocalChange carries it out as Option<u64> (zero reads as 'no time known', not as 1970), and the window shows a coarse relative time on both sides of the list -- the remote side already had at_unix and was not showing it either. Deliberately coarse: a save is not a stopwatch and a per-second string would be a reason to redraw forever. STILL NOT DONE: the remote ring still forgets on restart, which is the design and is defensible now that every row carries its own time; and nothing distinguishes added from changed, because the delta feed does not say.

UPDATE 2026-09-14: the sign-in and reboot halves are now done on Fedora, on a machine reinstalled that morning with nothing Cirrove needs pre-installed. The owner signed in at the console; the drive mounted under SELinux Enforcing with zero AVC denials of any kind across the whole boot (journalctl -b and ausearch), a 67794-byte file read end to end through FUSE with the right magic and byte count, the tray went Active and the shell drew it, Files showed the mount and the kept-offline badge, and all of it survived a reboot with nothing started by hand, pin included. That needs an Arch VM, which does not exist yet. UPDATE 2026-09-14 (Arch): the installation, reboot and removal halves are done on a clean Arch VM. The sign-in half is not, and is now the only thing outstanding on this row for any family -- Fedora has it, Ubuntu has it, Arch needs the owner at a browser once. READY 2026-09-15: the Arch VM is booted, running today's packages (r447) from CI, the service enabled and active with zero accounts -- which is the honest state of a fresh install and the state this row's last clause needs a person to change. Sign-in is at the VM's console: `CIRROVE_VM_DISPLAY=gtk scripts/vm/run.sh arch boot`, or vnc 127.0.0.1:12 while it is running, user `tester`, password `cirrove`. Everything else on this row is done for all three families. 2026-09-15, the Arch sign-in attempt, which found two things before it found an account and both were the same shape: something the other two families install with any desktop, that Arch does not, that Cirrove needed and had not declared. First `xdg-open` -- an optdepends -- so the Sign in button could not open a browser at all. Then, after a full Microsoft sign-in and a drive choice, `desktop Secret Service unavailable`: there was no keyring to keep the grant in, and the program only asked once the person's work was done. The owner's words: 'Diesen Fehler hatten wir doch schon bei Fedora! Wir müssen zu beginn schon prüfen ob es einen Schlüsselbund gibt' -- and they were right twice over. It HAD happened on Fedora, where the keyring was present and locked, and it was written off as a peculiarity of a machine that logs in automatically and put in the user guide rather than in the program. Both are now asked before the browser opens, in `DesktopVault::reachable`, and a locked keyring is offered to the desktop to unlock rather than merely reported. STILL NOT DONE: the Arch sign-in itself. DONE ON ARCH 2026-09-15, by the account owner at the machine. From the packages CI built for this branch on a clean Arch VM: the Cirrove window, Connect a drive, the application id typed in, Sign in with Microsoft, the browser inside the VM, consent, the drive chosen from the list the window showed -- and a mounted OneDrive. It then indexed the whole library, 184,080 items across both feeds, and a directory deep in the tree lists in 8 ms from the local index. The account came up `sign_in_required`, which is correct and is the automatic-login machine rather than the product: nobody typed a password, so nothing unlocked the keyring, and the daemon says so rather than pretending. After unlocking -- which a real login does -- ready, both feeds ready, files read. TWO DEFECTS FOUND ON THE WAY, both fixed the same day and both invisible to the other two families: xdg-utils was an optdepend so the sign-in button could not open a browser at all, and the Secret Service was only asked about AFTER the sign-in, so the first attempt threw away a completed Microsoft login. WHAT IS LEFT is not a sign-in: it is one clean-machine install of the FIXED package, to show pacman now brings xdg-utils with it. The sign-in itself does not need repeating. CI's build for ff2ab8f does: `pacman -Qip` on the built package reads `Depends On: fuse3 gcc-libs glibc xdg-utils`. rows.text: Upgrade/migration rollback protects settings, credentials and pending work.
rows.evidence: PARTIAL 2026-09-13. The data side is guarded and tested: the metadata store and the upload journal each carry a schema version, migrate forward inside one transaction that publishes the steps and the version together, and refuse a database newer than the build -- so an older package installed over a newer state stops with 'unsupported database schema version' rather than reading what it does not understand; migrations six, seven, eight and thirteen each keep pending work and are held to it; and a migration under a running daemon is refused (accounts::refuse_to_migrate_under_a_running_daemon, fail-closed on an unreadable file). Credentials live in the keyring under ids the settings file names and are touched by no migration. PACKAGE-LEVEL UPGRADE DONE 2026-09-13: cirrove and cirrove-desktop 0.1.0~dev.r351.ge9a91a4 upgraded in place to r370.g46de988 with apt in the Ubuntu VM, over a signed-in account. After the upgrade the account came back ready and mounted, the keyring grant was still readable, and the index still held all 184,053 items -- so nothing reindexed and no credential was lost across a real package upgrade. STILL NOT DONE: the same run with uploads pending at the moment of the upgrade, and the rollback -- install version N over N-1 on a machine with pending uploads, confirm they finish, roll back to N-1 and confirm it refuses cleanly rather than half-works; the settings file's version guard is held by accounts::tests::a_settings_file_from_a_newer_version_is_refused_rather_than_read. UPDATE 2026-09-14: measured with a live account rather than reasoned about, r409 to r418 and back on Fedora. Settings and credentials survive both directions -- the account still mounted with all 184053 items, the credential id byte-for-byte unchanged, the pin still resident, exactly one Files extension, and no sign-in asked for at any point. One defect found and fixed: the upgrade replaces the files and leaves the daemon and tray running from deleted binaries, so the person stays on the version they just replaced with nothing saying so; the daemon now reports restart_required and the window says it. The schema guard this row rests on was NOT exercised: r409 and r418 write the same format, so the rollback never met a newer state and nothing had to be refused. STILL NOT DONE: pending work, the third noun in the row -- the Fedora account is read-only, so nothing was queued to protect. That needs a write-consented account. See docs/benchmarks/upgrade-and-rollback.json. TICKED 2026-09-14. The third noun is now measured. On the Ubuntu VM with write consent, three files were written with the provider unreachable -- blocked at tcp/443 from inside, because pulling the virtual cable cuts ssh with it -- and queued as pending. apt-get install replaced both packages with all six journal entries naming them still present, the daemon was then restarted onto the new binary while they were still queued and they were still there, and 52 seconds after the provider returned all three finished with nobody retrying them. They were read back through the Fedora VM's mount of the same drive with their exact contents: a file the uploading daemon calls done is not evidence, a file another machine can read is. stuck_changes stayed 0 throughout -- waiting for a provider is pending, not stuck, and calling it stuck would send someone to discard work that was about to succeed. Files removed to the recycle bin afterwards. Settings and credentials were covered in the first run the same day.

The rollback half rests on the schema guards the store and the journal already carry and their unit tests; the measured rollback did not exercise them, because r409 and r370 write the same format, and that is recorded as unproven rather than passed.

rows.text: Clean uninstall and explicit retention/removal choices for local data. Measured on a machine with a live account and 2.6 GB of state ([the record](benchmarks/clean-uninstall.json)): nothing packaged survives, the person's data and their keyring grant are left alone, and the mount unmounts cleanly when the session ends. The choice is now the program's rather than the documentation's -- `cirrove local-data` reports what is kept and `--discard-removed` reclaims what an earlier removal set aside, which nothing had ever listed again.
rows.evidence: TICKED 2026-09-14 on a Fedora 44 VM with the owner's account mounted, one file pinned, a credential in an unlocked keyring and 2.6 GB of state; the packages were removed with all of it running, which is the honest case because nobody unmounts first. Clean: a find over /usr and /etc for anything named cirrove returned nothing, the state directory was untouched, the keyring grant survived labelled 'Cirrove Microsoft account' so a person can find it, and stopping the service -- what logging out does -- unmounted cleanly with no stale handle. One oddity recorded rather than fixed: the removal leaves the daemon running from a deleted binary still serving the mount until the session ends, which is untidy but not dangerous, and the window's new restart banner is the nearest thing that speaks to it. The retention/removal choice was the real gap and is now closed: `cirrove forget` has always set a removed connection's data aside instead of deleting it, and nothing ever listed it again, so an uninstall left gigabytes the person believed they had removed. `cirrove local-data` reports each connection, anything set aside, and the total; `--discard-removed` deletes only the set-aside part and says how much it freed.
rows.asserted_by: cirrove-service tests/accounts_local_data.rs: set-aside data is reported with its size and the timestamp parsed from its directory name and counts as the reclaimable total while a live account's does not; discard_set_aside removes it and leaves a live account's cache file present, which is the safety property the whole feature turns on; and an empty removed/ deletes nothing and does not fail. The dangerous version of this command is one that could be talked into deleting a drive still in use, and it is not reachable from any argument.

rows.text: Validate the desktop entry, installed icons and AppStream metainfo in CI, then compare their identity with the running window and application bus name in the supported desktop sessions. Current desktop-file validation alone does not satisfy this gate.
rows.evidence: PARTIAL 2026-09-13. CI now validates both desktop entries with desktop-file-validate and the AppStream metainfo with appstreamcli validate, and runs the identity test that ties them to the tray's bus name. NOT DONE: the comparison with the running window's app_id and bus name in the supported desktop sessions; CI has Xvfb only and no complete GNOME or Plasma session, so that half waits on the session matrix. TICKED 2026-09-14. The runtime half is now a check that runs on every push rather than one that waited for a desktop. CI has Xvfb, which is an X server, and the window scenarios already run under it -- so the X11 identity is read off a running window with xprop, exactly the way a shell reads it, with x11-utils added to the job for the tool. The scenario declines to assert where there is no pure X11 display, because under Wayland the identity is the app_id and checking WM_CLASS through Xwayland would be testing Xwayland. The comparison was also made by hand in all four sessions of the matrix: Hyprland and KWin on Wayland by app_id, GNOME Xorg and Plasma X11 by WM_CLASS. That is where the defect was found -- the window announced itself as 'cirrove-desktop' against an entry named io.github.Dandiccf.Cirrove.desktop -- and where the fix was confirmed.
rows.asserted_by: The CI step 'Desktop entries and AppStream metainfo are valid' in .github/workflows/ci.yml, plus desktop::packaging::the_desktop_entry_icon_and_metainfo_share_one_application_identity. cirrove-desktop tests/window.rs the_x11_window_class_is_the_application_id_a_shell_looks_for reads WM_CLASS from a running window with xprop and requires the application id. Shown to fail with the identity removed. It also found a fault in the first fix: setting the program name in main.rs meant anything building the window another way got the binary's name and the class came out empty under the harness, so it now lives on Window::APP_ID beside the constructor, and tests/packaging.rs holds that constant to the desktop entry's name.

rows.text: Build and install the daemon and CLI without GTK4/libadwaita present, with separate desktop packaging. The root's default members now exclude the desktop; explicit `--workspace` builds and full contributor checks still include it. A package installation on a clean headless host remains required; headless buildability does not imply unattended browser/keyring setup.
rows.evidence: DONE 2026-09-13. Headless buildability was already checked: the mounted-read-workloads CI job installs neither libgtk-4-dev nor libadwaita-1-dev, asserts their absence, builds the daemon and CLI in release and runs the CLI. What was missing was the other half -- a package installation on a host that has no desktop -- because the deb and rpm jobs install onto runners where the desktop libraries were installed minutes earlier to build the desktop package, so they could say the Depends field names no desktop library but not that the daemon runs without one. The headless-package-install job now installs the core package alone into a clean ubuntu:24.04 container: it fails first if the container already has libgtk-4 or libadwaita, so the test cannot pass vacuously; installs with --no-install-recommends, because the package recommends gnome-keyring and xdg-utils and pulling them in would test apt's defaults rather than what the daemon requires; asserts afterwards that nothing GTK arrived and that neither binary names one in NEEDED; runs both; then installs the desktop package in the same container and asserts the opposite, that GTK does arrive and cirrove-desktop links it -- so the split is shown in both directions rather than only the direction that is easy to pass; and finally purges and checks nothing survives. Every step green on CI run 34762849239 (2026-09-13). Separate desktop packaging is the cirrove/cirrove-desktop split those jobs install.
rows.asserted_by: CI job headless-package-install for the packaged install on a desktop-free host, and mounted-read-workloads for the build; the root's default members exclude the desktop crate, held by the workspace manifest.
